Performer: Shannon Norman, Chicken, Roy J Gloeckl II, Alyssa Maurer, Andrew Hilary

Join us for a night of laughter with a cause.

Local cat-loving comedians are "feline funny" and coming together at Steel City Cellar for an evening of cat jokes, stories and camaraderie. Ticket sales for this event (and a possible raffle TBA) will benefit Pittsburgh-based rescue, Oakland TNR Coalition.

Host, Meghan "Chicken" Tutolo takes the stage along with 6 hilarious cat-crazy comics in the name of helping cats in our city. If this goes well, we will continue to host Feline Funny events that benefit other local rescues, so please come out in support!

Cat sweaters optional, but encouraged.

CAST OF CAT-LOVING COMICS
Jared Figel
Roy Gloeckl
Andrew Hilary
Alyssa Maurer
Shannon Norman
Effie Stone
Meghan "Chicken" Tutolo, Host

ABOUT OAKLAND TNR COALITION
Oakland TNR Coalition is a 100% volunteer-run, grassroots 501(c)(3) nonprofit dedicated to improving the lives of cats in Oakland, Pittsburgh, and the surrounding communities through Trap-Neuter-Return (TNR), rescue, rehabilitation, adoption and education.

Learn more about Oakland TNR Coalition: https://www.oaklandtnrcoalition.org

Feline Funny is a Cross the Road Comedy production.

Pittsburgh Symphony’s 2026–27 Season Balances Familiar Faces and New Directions

Pittsburgh Symphony’s 2026–27 Season Balances Familiar Faces and New Directions

By
ghoover

on

February 10, 2026
•
(
1
)

The PSO’s newly announced 2026–27 classical season leans into what the ensemble does best: deep artistic relationships, ambitious programming, and a growing interest in how symphonic music fits into contemporary cultural life.

Music Director
Manfred Honeck
returns for his 19th season with the orchestra, leading a lineup that includes nine artist debuts, multiple premieres and commissions, and season-long explorations of Beethoven and Mozart.

“After almost 19 years together, what continues to inspire me most is the depth of trust and curiosity we share as an orchestra,” said Honeck. “This season reflects that spirit of the artistic mission and its intensity, where we stand side by side to challenge and inspire one another. I am restless in my search for the essential meaning of the music and am grateful to our wonderful musicians that they are so devoted in this exploration.”

An Orchestra Built on Continuity

Honeck’s long tenure has allowed the PSO to cultivate a sense of artistic continuity that’s increasingly rare among major American orchestras. That continuity shows up this season in the return of conductors who have become familiar collaborators in Pittsburgh, including Dima Slobodeniouk, Petr Popelka, Daniele Rustioni, Juraj Valčuha, Elim Chan, and Donald Runnicles.

Soloists range from internationally recognized names—
Lang Lang
,
Augustin Hadelich
,
Sheku Kanneh-Mason
,
Jeanine De Bique
, and
Kirill Gerstein
—to artists making their first appearances with the orchestra. Over the course of the season, audiences will hear 10 pianists and five violin soloists, reflecting the orchestra’s ongoing interest in instrumental voices.

PSO Musicians Take Center Stage

Several programs spotlight the PSO’s own musicians. Principal Tuba
Craig Knox
premieres a new concerto written for him by composer
Nick DiBerardino
, commissioned by the orchestra. Principal Clarinet
Michael Rusinek
is featured in Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto during a recording weekend that also includes Mahler’s Symphony No. 1.

Choral collaborations return as well, with the
Mendelssohn Choir of Pittsburgh
joining the orchestra for Beethoven’s
Mass in C major
—a PSO premiere—in December 2026, followed by Orff’s
Carmina Burana
in February 2027.

New Voices, Contemporary Music

The season continues the PSO’s commitment to living composers and emerging artists. Conductors
Karina Canellakis
,
Kevin John Edusei
, and
Kahchun Wong
make their PSO debuts, along with first appearances by pianist
Alexander Malofeev
, violinists
Francesca Dego
and
Tessa Lark
, mezzo-soprano J
ulie Boulianne
, soprano
Joelle Harvey
, and baritone
Will Liverman
.

Contemporary works by Anna Clyne, Mason Bates, Victoria Borisova, Camille Pépin, and Arvo Pärt are woven throughout the season, with 10 PSO premieres in total. New commissions include a work by Bates, DiBerardino’s tuba concerto, and a new operatic suite based on Korngold’s
Die tote Stadt
by Honeck and longtime collaborator Tomas Ille. The orchestra also joins peer institutions as a co-commissioner on new works by Juri Reinvere, Samy Moussa, and Carlos Simon.

Beethoven, Mozart, and Big Ideas

Beethoven’s music forms a connective thread throughout the season as the PSO marks the 200th anniversary of the composer’s death. Highlights include a March program pairing Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony with the Violin Concerto, performed by Hadelich, and a U.S. premiere by Reinvere inspired by Beethoven’s final words.

In April 2027, the orchestra shifts to Mozart for an All-Mozart weekend featuring pianist Rudolf Buchbinder. Two programs include Piano Concertos Nos. 20 and 21 and Symphonies Nos. 40 and 41, alongside live-orchestra performances of
Amadeus
, conducted by Associate Conductor Jacob Joyce.

The Concert Experience, Reimagined

The PSO continues to fold elements of its recent experimental series into the core subscription experience. Live video, expanded program notes, onstage commentary, and pre- and post-concert performances are now regular features of many weekends. Standalone series such as
Disrupt
and
Saturday Sessions
will not continue, but their influence remains visible in the orchestra’s evolving approach to presentation.

Looking Ahead

Select concerts will be recorded for future releases, including Mahler’s Symphony No. 1, Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto, Korngold’s
Die tote Stadt
, and Sibelius’ Symphony No. 2, extending a recording legacy that has earned the eleven GRAMMY nominations in recent years.

Subscriptions for the BNY Classics series are now available, with single tickets expected later this summer. Additional announcements—including Pops, Fiddlesticks, Schooltime programs, and the previously revealed 2026 Cinematic Summer Festival—will be released in the coming months.

Review: Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra Welcomes New Season with a Goodbye

Review: Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra Welcomes New Season with a Goodbye

By
Jim Lewis

on

October 4, 2026
•
(
0
)

By JAMES H. LEWIS

The
Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestr
a welcomes concertgoers to its 2026-2027 season with a stunning performance at
Heinz Hall
this weekend while bidding adieu to one of its most beloved musicians.

Most orchestral concerts follow a familiar pattern: an introductory piece is followed by a concerto in three movements featuring a solo artist. After the intermission, the concert concludes with a full four-movement symphony. This weekend’s performance flipped the order, presenting the symphony before the intermission and returning with the concerto.

One reason for this is that
Felix Mendelssohn
’s Symphony #4
in A Major (the Italian) is comparatively brief, lasting just under half an hour, while
Johannes Brahms’

Piano Concerto #2
in B-flat major is in four movements and lasts nearly twice as long. That, however, was only part of the reason for the switch.

The performance opened with a short piece,
Masquerade
, by contemporary British composer
Anna Clyne
, which Maestro
Manfred Honeck
praised as he introduced it. First performed at the Last Night of the Proms by the
BBC Symphony
under the direction of American
Marin Alsop
, the piece consists of a series of cascading chord progressions, linked by glissandi, which is passed from one section to another. It quickly resolves into an English country dance melody, presented once in traditional form, and returns as a tango.

Mendelssohn conceived Symphony #4 during a winter and spring he spent in Italy. He called it the most amusing piece he had written to that point, but continued to revise it during his lifetime and was still not satisfied at his death. Yet it remains a remarkable piece. The opening movement, allegro vivace, is one of Mendelssohn’s most familiar and beloved themes, played at a breakneck pace. Woodwinds state an opening, which the strings develop into an initial theme. The full orchestra joins in, playing a fortissimo section that descends into a quiet recitation of the original theme.

The second movement begins as a scherzo, introducing a second theme which the sections pass along themselves fuguelike. The third movement is in three-quarter time, a minuet, followed by the final movement, a rollicking dance number that recalls the theme and lightheartedness of the first, but with more intensity. The symphony ends with a final fortissimo climax that brought the audience to its feet.

Gerstein Kirill
(Image courtsey PSO)

Brahms’ Piano Concerto was performed by
Gerstein

Kirill,
an American pianist born in the former Soviet Union. Gerstein, who is now Professor of Piano at the
Hanns Eisler Hochschule
in Berlin, made his orchestral debut performing Brahms’s
Piano Concerto No. 1,
and this weekend turned his attention to its successor, which Brahms wrote two decades later.

The piano enters immediately in the first,
allegro non troppo
movement, then plays a duet with a solo horn introducing the first theme before the full orchestra joins in stating a lyrical second. The interplay between horn and piano reemerges to present a lyrical restatement of the second theme and a triumphant climax.

The second movement,
allegro appasianato
, presents the third theme, with Gerstein executing a complex pianissimo passage in double octaves. The pace increases to breakneck speed and a dramatic close.

Anne Martindale Williams
(Image courtsey PSO)

From the first notes of the
andante
third movement, the other reason for the placement of the concerto at the end of the performance became apparent. The lyrical piece opens with the piano playing a duet with a single cello, performed by
Anne Martindale Williams.
This is her final performance with the PSO. She began her career fifty years ago as Associate Principal Cellist under
William Steinberg. André Previn
appointed her Principal three years later
,
a position she has held ever since. In marking her retirement, President and CEO
Melia Tourangeau
put it simply: “She devoted her entire career to the PSO.” The movement ended with an extended duet between the two artists.

The final movement, which began without interruption, opened as a dance with sections reminiscent of Brahms’ Hungarian rhapsodies. Gerstein performed a deft right-handed series of octaves that ended the concerto with a burst of joy.

As he and Honeck took their bows, Gerstein reached for Williams’ hand and brought her forward to stand with him. He took two more curtain calls, insisting that she join him and Honeck for both.

It was a fitting tribute to one of the orchestra’s most treasured musicians, one who broke the glass ceiling at a time when the section leaders of almost every major symphony orchestra were male. The PSO will miss her artistry, kindness, and ever-present smile.

The PSO’s classical series resumes Friday, October 16, and Sunday, October 18, with Rachmaninoff’s Symphony #2.

James Lewis is a former public media professional and consultant who now writes fiction. Many of his eleven novels are set in Pittsburgh, his adopted home.

Charlie Wallace: The Stars Are Watching

Skip to get tickets

Charlie Wallace: The Stars Are Watching

Fri, Oct 30 - Sun, Apr 11, 2027

Pittsburgh Cultural Trust

707 Gallery

Ticket Prices

Free

Free

Visual Arts

The Pittsburgh Cultural Trust is pleased to present its fourth exhibition in collaboration with VaultArt Studios, a Pittsburgh-based non-profit and project of Achieva dedicated to providing a professional studio environment for artists with disabilities. This ongoing partnership reflects a sustained institutional commitment to expanding the field of contemporary art by ensuring that artists with disabilities are not positioned at its margins, but are recognized as vital contributors to its present and future.
This exhibition features a new body of work by Charlie Wallace, a founding member of VaultArt Studio, whose practice engages deeply with the visual language of celebrity culture and is distinguished by his large-scale, meticulously rendered paper doll compositions. For this presentation, Wallace turns his attention to the Major Arcana of the tarot—a sequence of 22 cards that have, for centuries, functioned as a symbolic system for mapping human experience, transformation, and fate.
Across art history, tarot imagery has served as a rich site of interpretation, from its origins in Renaissance Europe to its reimagining by modern and contemporary artists drawn to its dense layering of allegory, mysticism, and psychological insight. The Major Arcana in particular can be understood as a set of enduring archetypes—The Fool, The Magician, The Lovers, Death–figures that articulate universal narratives of beginnings, power, desire, loss, and renewal.
Wallace reinterprets these archetypes through the lens of contemporary celebrity, translating each card into a carefully constructed likeness of a cultural icon. In doing so, he collapses distinctions between mythic and mediated identities, inviting viewers to consider how celebrity itself functions as a modern system of archetype—one through which collective aspirations, anxieties, and projections are continually performed and circulated. His signature two dimensional portrait format further underscores this dynamic, emphasizing themes of construction, projection, and transformation inherent to both tarot and celebrity culture alike.
Charlie Wallace is guest curated by Steph Neary, VaultArt Studios in collaboration with the Pittsburgh Cultural Trust.
